Hodgkinson9:00 AM CST on November 4, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleAlmost exactly a century ago, in October 1926, Cambridge University made a small but significant change to its statutes. It introduced the right for academics to take every seventh term off.The word “sabbatical” comes from the Hebrew shabbat, meaning “rest.” Yet in an academic context, it usually means a rest from one kind of work, so that you can focus on another. Cambridge’s embrace of the sabbatical was a sign that the university didn’t only care about teaching students. It also wanted its scholars to carry out original research. This innovation was just one milestone among many in the slow process by which the very purpose of our universities was gradually altered—a transformation that was driven by a mysterious-sounding group of British scientists who called themselves the “X Club.” Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
